input: The Prandtl number is a dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in heat transfer, and it can be defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. To understand what this really means, it helps to think about what each of these diffusivities actually does. Momentum diffusivity is essentially a measure of how rapidly a difference in velocity is smoothed out within a flowing fluid, while thermal diffusivity is a measure of how rapidly a difference in temperature is smoothed out. The Prandtl number therefore brings these two tendencies together into a single figure that allows them to be compared directly. If the value is close to 1, this tells us that the two diffusivities are of a similar size, so momentum and heat spread through the fluid at broadly comparable rates, and the velocity field and the temperature field develop in a broadly similar way. At the other extreme, if the Prandtl number is large, momentum diffusivity is much greater than thermal diffusivity, which means that momentum spreads much more readily than heat does; the velocity field is smoothed out over distances over which the temperature field changes hardly at all, and a temperature difference can persist within a comparatively thin layer. It is important to note that, because the Prandtl number is a ratio, it does not by itself say anything about the actual size of either diffusivity, and two different fluids could in principle share the same Prandtl number while differing in both of the underlying diffusivities quite considerably. A Prandtl number of exactly 1 would represent the special case in which the two diffusivities are identical, and values progressively further above 1 represent cases in which the momentum diffusivity is progressively more dominant over its thermal counterpart.
target: The Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity measures how fast a velocity difference is evened out within a fluid; thermal diffusivity measures how fast a temperature difference is evened out. The Prandtl number compares the two rates for one fluid under one set of conditions. A value near 1 means the two rates are close: momentum and heat spread through the fluid at comparable speeds, and the velocity and temperature fields develop together, so a disturbance in either is smoothed over much the same distance. A large value means momentum diffusivity is much the larger of the two. Momentum then spreads far more readily than heat; the velocity field is evened out over distances across which the temperature field is barely smoothed, and a temperature difference persists in a layer much thinner than the layer across which the velocity changes. The number is a ratio, and it states nothing about either diffusivity on its own: two fluids can share a Prandtl number while differing in both diffusivities, because the number fixes only the proportion between them. What the proportion governs is the relative shape of the velocity and temperature fields, and that is the whole content of the definition. Read in that way, the Prandtl number sorts fluids by behaviour rather than by size: near 1, the two fields are alike in extent; well above 1, the temperature field is the confined one, and the velocity field reaches across ground the temperature field does not.
